feed.subtitle: Jianyu Fu (付舰于), Ph.D. student at The University of Tokyo, researches human mobility, urban perception, geospatial data science, and multimodal AI for sustainable cities.

entry.title: Mapping streetscape emotions in Landscape and Urban Planning (IF 11.5)

link.title: Mapping streetscape emotions in Landscape and Urban Planning (IF 11.5)

entry.content:
Our paper, “Evaluating urban street views through collective emotional perception from multimodal social media cityscape posts: An R-ECoT-based interpretable framework,” was published online on 3 November 2026 in Landscape and Urban Planning (Elsevier; JCR Q1 · Impact Factor 11.5). DOI: 10.1016/j.landurbplan.2026.105822.

I led this study as a doctoral researcher in the Sekimoto Lab at The University of Tokyo, with Xukang Wang, Jue Ma, Chenbo Zhao, Yoshiki Ogawa, and Yoshihide Sekimoto.

Learning from comments on city photographs

What can the comments beneath a street photograph tell us about how people see that place? Through approved access to the Meta Content Library API in the SOMAR Virtual Data Enclave, we analyzed 1,078 Facebook and Instagram cityscape posts and 20,546 comments. We used the comments to estimate the strength of Plutchik’s eight emotions for each photograph. A single scene could evoke several emotions at once, something a single positive or negative label would miss.

We used these estimates to train R-ECoT, a vision–language model that predicts an emotion profile from an image alone. For each prediction, it also highlights the parts of the photograph that contributed most. This makes it possible to inspect, for example, which parts of the same scene the model associates with joy and which it associates with fear.

From photographs to a street map

Across the models we tested, the CLIP-based version of R-ECoT performed best: KL divergence 0.329, mean squared error 0.0106, and balanced accuracy 0.757. We then applied it to 610,017 ZENRIN street-view images in Setagaya Ward, Tokyo, and aggregated predictions along 10-metre road segments.

These maps show how the model interprets visible street conditions. They do not measure the feelings of individual pedestrians. For a planner, their value is in finding a segment worth visiting and then tracing its score back to the photograph: which features drew the model’s attention, and do they merit a closer look on site?
entry.summary: R-ECoT uses public responses to cityscape photographs to estimate eight emotions and map them along streets in Setagaya, Tokyo.

entry.title: Tokyo streetscape study accepted for IEEE BigData 2026

link.title: Tokyo streetscape study accepted for IEEE BigData 2026

entry.content:
On 3 November 2026, our paper “Beyond Top-Down Urban Sensing: Cross-View Explanatory Asymmetry in Image-Estimated Streetscape Perception in Tokyo” (SP06202) was accepted for presentation at the Special Session on Neo Urban Metabolism at IEEE BigData 2026. The China Computer Federation lists the main conference as CCF-C.

The study asks whether a satellite view and a street-level view of the same Tokyo neighbourhood explain the same aspects of streetscape perception. We align the two perspectives on a 100-metre grid and compare how much each adds when the other is already available.
entry.summary: Paper SP06202 was accepted for presentation at the Special Session on Neo Urban Metabolism.

entry.title: Paper accepted in Landscape and Urban Planning

link.title: Paper accepted in Landscape and Urban Planning

entry.content:
Our paper “Evaluating urban street views through collective emotional perception from multimodal social media cityscape posts: An R-ECoT-based interpretable framework” was accepted by Landscape and Urban Planning on 23 October 2026.

JCR Q1 · Impact Factor 11.5

Authors: Jianyu Fu, X. Wang, J. Ma, C. Zhao, Y. Ogawa, and Y. Sekimoto. I am the first and corresponding author.

Update, 3 November 2026: The article is now online. Read the research introduction or open the published paper.
entry.summary: Our R-ECoT paper was accepted on 23 October 2026. JCR Q1 · Impact Factor 11.5. Published online on 3 November 2026.

entry.title: Research visit to The University of Hong Kong

link.title: Research visit to The University of Hong Kong

entry.content:
From 5 August to 10 October 2026, I visited the Department of Geography, The University of Hong Kong, as a visiting Ph.D. researcher, hosted by Prof. Bo Huang.

During the visit, I conducted collaborative research on urban mobility and human behavior, focusing on spatial patterns of individual travel-time burdens in Greater Paris. The work combined a sanitized GNSS-based mobility dataset with urban spatial information to examine differences in observed travel experiences.

The related manuscript, “When mobility continues at a cost: Individual travel-time burdens in Greater Paris,” is under review. I am grateful to Prof. Huang and the team for their support and discussions during the visit.
entry.summary: A visiting Ph.D. research stay with Prof. Bo Huang in the Department of Geography, from 5 August to 10 October 2026.
